summary: Gives recommendations for jittering, or randomly adjusting, control message timing in mobile ad hoc network routing protocols, to reduce collisions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When two wireless devices send at the same moment, the messages collide and neither gets through. The memo recommends adding a small random delay to control messages so that neighbours are unlikely to send together, and says how big that delay may be.

what is jitter in manet protocols
why add random delay to manet messages
subtitle: Add a little randomness to when wireless routers send control messages, so neighbours stop talking over each other.

tldr.problem: In a wireless network, two nearby nodes that transmit at the same time collide, and the receiver loses the packets. Several common routing-protocol behaviours make such simultaneous transmissions likely.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends jitter, a deliberate random variation in timing, applied in three places: shortening the interval between periodic messages, delaying triggered messages, and delaying forwarded messages. Each uses a MAXJITTER parameter that bounds how much the timing can vary.
tldr.outcome: The document is Informational and generalizes the mechanism used by the OLSR routing protocol. It sets the rules a protocol has to follow if it uses jitter, including how the random values are drawn and how large MAXJITTER may be.

facts.label: Maximum jitter with a minimum interval

today: RFC 5148 is an Informational document published in February 2008, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It generalizes the jitter mechanism used by the OLSR routing protocol, described in RFC 3626, and leaves the choice of concrete values to the protocols that adopt it.

sections.title: Why Simultaneous Transmissions Are a Problem
sections.content:
In a wireless network, simultaneous packet transmission by nearby nodes is often undesirable, because any resulting collision between those packets may make a receiving node fail to receive some or all of them. This is a physical problem that occurs before the packets can even be inserted into the receiver's queue. Depending on the characteristics of the medium access control and other lower-layer mechanisms, and in particular on whether retransmission of unacknowledged packets is supported, this may cause at best increased delay and at worst complete packet loss. Some instances of the problem can be solved in those lower layers, but in other cases some help at the network and higher layers is necessary.

This document considers the case where that help is required and gives recommendations for using jitter, which is randomly varying timing, to provide it. The techniques described could be implemented either by IP protocols designed for wireless networks or in conjunction with lower-layer mechanisms.

The problems of simultaneous transmission are amplified by four features of a protocol. Regularly scheduled messages: if two nodes generate packets containing regularly scheduled messages of the same type at the same time, and use the same message interval as is typical, all further transmissions of those messages will also be at the same time. Event-triggered messages: if nodes respond to changes in their circumstances, in particular changes in their neighbourhood, with immediate message generation and transmission, then two nearby nodes that respond to the same change will transmit at the same time. Schedule reset: when a node sends an event-triggered message of a type that is usually regularly scheduled, there is no apparent reason why it should not restart its corresponding message schedule, which may mean nodes responding to the same change also send future messages simultaneously. And forwarding: if nodes forward messages they receive from other nodes, nearby nodes will commonly receive and forward the same message, and if forwarding is done immediately the resulting transmissions may interfere with each other.

The possible solution is to employ jitter, a deliberate random variation in timing. Jitter is used elsewhere, in OSPF, in host group extensions for CLNP multicasting and in BGP, where transmission intervals for regularly scheduled messages are reduced by a small, bounded and random amount in order to desynchronize transmitters and thereby avoid overloading the transmission medium as well as receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: Two radios talking at once means neither message arrives. Jitter nudges each sender by a random amount so that the odds of two neighbours picking the same instant are low, and so that a collision does not repeat every round.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
A node is a MANET router that implements a message sending protocol, and a MANET interface is a network device taking part in the MANET; a node may have one or more of them. A message is an entity carrying protocol information intended for exchange between nodes, and messages are transmitted over MANET interfaces embedded in packets. A packet is an entity embedding zero or more messages for transmission over a MANET interface. A transmission is a packet being sent over a MANET interface, whether due to a message being generated or forwarded. Generation is the creation of a new message rather than a received and forwarded one, and a node will typically generate messages based on a message schedule, periodic or otherwise, or as a response to changes in circumstances. Forwarding is the retransmission of a received message, modified or unchanged, over one or more MANET interfaces.

A collision is a specific instance of interference where two or more nodes transmit a packet at the same time and within the same signal space, at the same frequency or encoding, such that another, closely located node that should receive and decode those packets instead fails to do so and loses one or more of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is careful about words. A message is the protocol information, a packet is what goes on the air, a transmission is one packet leaving one interface, and a collision is two of those landing at the same instant so that the intended receiver loses one.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.content:
The mechanisms described are applicable to the control messages of any MANET protocol in which simultaneous transmissions by different nodes are undesirable, and which contains mechanisms, such as periodic control message transmission, triggered control message transmission or control message forwarding, that either make a simultaneous transmission more likely or cause one to be repeated when it occurs. This particularly applies to protocols using broadcast transmissions in wireless networks: proactive MANET routing protocols such as OLSR employ scheduled messages, reactive MANET routing protocols such as AODV employ event-triggered messages, and both employ message forwarding.

The mechanisms are intended for use where the underlying medium access control and lower layers do not provide effective ways to avoid such collisions. Where those layers do provide effective mechanisms, the recommendations of this document are not needed. The approach uses random variations in timing to reduce collisions; alternatives using pseudo-random variation based on node identity may be considered but are not discussed here. Any protocol based on the Generalized MANET Packet/Message Format and using the message forwarding mechanism that structure facilitates is a particular candidate for at least some of these mechanisms. The document has been generalized from the jitter mechanism used in the proactive MANET routing protocol OLSR.
sections.plainLanguage: Use this when the radio layer cannot sort out the collisions itself. It matters most for protocols that broadcast regular beacons, that react instantly to a change nearby, or that relay other people's messages, which is most of them.

sections.title: The Three Jitter Mechanisms
sections.content:
To prevent nodes in a MANET from transmitting simultaneously while keeping the MANET characteristic of maximum node autonomy, a randomization of the transmission time of packets by nodes, known as jitter, should be employed. Three jitter mechanisms target different aspects of the problem and should be used, with the aim of reducing the likelihood of simultaneous transmission and, if it occurs, preventing it from continuing. For periodic message generation, jitter reduces the interval between successive message transmissions by a random amount; for the other two cases, jitter delays a message being generated or forwarded by a random amount. Each case uses a parameter, denoted MAXJITTER, for the maximum timing variation it introduces, and a protocol may use the same or different values of MAXJITTER for each case, for each message type and under different circumstances.

For periodic message generation, two successive messages are separated by a well-defined interval, the message interval, and a node may maintain more than one such interval for different message types or circumstances, such as backing off transmissions to avoid congestion. Jitter should be applied by reducing this delay by a random amount, so the delay between consecutive transmissions of messages of the same type is the message interval minus the jitter. Subtracting rather than adding ensures the interval never exceeds the message interval and does not adversely affect timeouts or other mechanisms based on a message arriving late or failing to arrive. Basing the transmission time on the previous transmission time, rather than jittering a fixed clock, lets nodes become completely desynchronized, which minimizes the probability of repeated collisions; this is particularly useful combined with externally triggered message generation and rescheduling. The jitter value should be generated uniformly in an interval between zero and MAXJITTER.

For externally triggered message generation, an internal or external condition or event may trigger generation of a single message, including an acknowledgement, the start of a new periodic message schedule, or the rescheduling of existing periodic messaging. Collisions between triggered messages become more likely if more than one node is likely to respond to the same event. To reduce that likelihood, an externally triggered message should be jittered by delaying it by a random duration; an internally triggered message may be jittered too. The delay should be generated uniformly between zero and MAXJITTER. If periodically transmitted messages are rescheduled, this should be based on the delayed time, with subsequent messages treated as in the periodic case. A protocol may also impose a minimum interval between messages of the same type, the message minimum interval, which is considered to be zero when not required; when it is non-zero it is appropriate to allow it to be reduced by jitter as well. It may look counterintuitive to define a minimum interval and then allow jitter to reduce it, but in a highly dynamic network with triggered messages the external circumstances may be more frequent than the minimum interval, which then takes the role of the message interval as the default interval at which messages are sent, and jittering it avoids synchronization.

For message forwarding, a node should delay the forwarding by a random duration generated uniformly between zero and MAXJITTER. Unlike the other two cases, a node forwarding a message is not automatically aware of the originator's message interval, which is needed to pick a MAXJITTER known to be valid; this may require prior agreement, inclusion of the message interval in the message, or another protocol-specific mechanism, including estimating it from received message times. A node may also receive a message while still waiting to forward an earlier message of the same type from the same node, which is possible without jitter but may occur more often with it, and the right action is protocol-specific, typically to discard the earlier message or to forward both. Where messages are transmitted hop by hop in multi-message packets, the forwarding should be in a single packet for efficiency, and the forwarding jitter of all messages received in a single packet should be the same, which requires a single value of MAXJITTER and a single random jitter for all of them; giving each message its own random jitter and taking the smallest produces a non-uniform distribution and a reduced mean.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three places to add randomness. Shorten the gap between regular beacons by a random amount, delay a message triggered by an event, or delay relaying someone else's message. All three draw a random number between zero and a maximum, and the random number is subtracted from the interval rather than added, so nothing is ever sent late.

sections.title: Choosing the Maximum Jitter
sections.content:
Jitter may resolve the problem of simultaneous transmissions, but the timing changes, and in particular the delays, it introduces will typically have a negative impact on a well-designed protocol, so MAXJITTER should always be minimized, subject to acceptably achieving its intent. For periodically generated messages, every relevant instance of MAXJITTER must not be negative, must not be greater than the message interval divided by two, and should not be greater than the message interval divided by four. If the message minimum interval is greater than zero, MAXJITTER must not be greater than it and should not be greater than half of it.

The choice should also suit the medium access control and lower layers. MAXJITTER should be significantly greater than, for example an order of magnitude greater than, any medium access control frame period. Because jitter is meant to reduce collisions, a larger value is appropriate when the chance of collisions is greater, which is particularly the case with increased node density, significant relative to the square of the interference range rather than the useful signal range. The value used when forwarding may also take into account the expected number of times a message will be sequentially forwarded, up to the network diameter in hops, so that the maximum accumulated delay is bounded.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the random delay as small as possible while still doing the job. For regular messages it should be no more than half the sending interval, and preferably a quarter of it, and it should be far larger than the time the radio layer takes to send one frame.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document provides recommendations for mechanisms to be used in protocols; full security considerations are to be provided by those protocols rather than here. It does note one side effect: the introduction of random timing by these recommendations may give a protocol some security advantage, because it makes the prediction of transmission times, and thereby intentional interference through selectively scheduling jamming transmissions to coincide with protocol message transmissions, more difficult.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo leaves security to the protocols that use it, but points out one benefit of random timing: an attacker finds it harder to work out when to jam the channel on purpose.

viz.caption: FOUR PROTOCOL FEATURES THAT AMPLIFY COLLISIONS

items.title: Regularly scheduled messages
items.text: Two nodes with the same interval keep sending at the same moment, round after round.

items.title: Event-triggered messages
items.text: Two nearby nodes that react to the same change react at the same instant.

items.title: Schedule reset
items.text: A triggered message can restart the schedule, putting neighbours back in step.

items.title: Forwarding
items.text: Neighbours receive the same message and relay it at the same moment.

viz.caption: THE THREE PLACES TO APPLY JITTER

cells: Reduce the message interval by the jitter
Delay the message by the jitter
Delay the forwarding by the jitter

items.title: At most half the interval
items.text: For periodic messages, MAXJITTER must not exceed the message interval divided by two.

items.title: Prefer a quarter
items.text: It should not exceed the message interval divided by four.

items.title: Minimum interval
items.text: With a non-zero minimum interval, MAXJITTER must not exceed it, and should not exceed half of it.
